events.name: A Window into the Ptolemaic Mind:
events.description:
Speaker: Orly Goldwasser

Woman Classifiers in the Egyptian Script

This lecture is part of the ISAW Library events series and will take place in person at ISAW (15 East 84th Street). Registration is required; click through for the registration link. This lecture explores a new source of evidence for the status and conceptualization of women in Ptolemaic Egypt through a pilot study of classifiers in the hieroglyphic system. From the Old Kingdom onwards, Egyptian hieroglyphic writing employed a highly organized system of category markers—classifiers or determinatives. These “mute” hieroglyphs, typically placed at the end of words, provide a unique window onto the emic organization of knowledge and the categories through which the ancient Egyptians conceptualized their world.

events.name: Burial and Betrayal
events.description:
Speaker: Darcy Tuttle

Punishing Social Transgressions in the Ancient Roman Cemetery

This lecture will take place in person at ISAW. Registration is required; click through for the registration link. The ancient Roman cemetery is often framed as the domain of the “well deserving,” as funerary monuments frequently formulaically assert. These dead were deserving of proper burial, of commemoration, and of the ongoing provision of offerings and other cult activities that both integrated them into the community of the dead and maintained their relationships with the living. But what might happen to the “badly deserving?” By examining select case studies of social betrayal documented in Roman cemeteries from the first three centuries CE, this talk will explore efforts at enforcing postmortem punishments against those perceived to have violated Roman social norms. It will argue that these stories of betrayal, while unique in their specifics, together illuminate the ways in which private individuals could seek to impose a form of afterlife exile upon those they deemed guilty of social transgressions.

events.name: Exhibition Lecture: Cursing, Curing, Creating: The Culture of Magic in Ancient Egypt
events.description:
Speaker: Foy Scalf

This lecture will take place in person at ISAW. Registration is required; click through for the registration link. For the ancient Egyptians, magic was not an illicit alternative to religion or a mysterious violation of the natural world. Heka—the force usually translated as “magic”—was woven into creation itself and provided gods and humans with the causative power to make things happen. Drawing on texts and objects featured in the ISAW exhibition Cursed! The Power of Magic in the Ancient World, this lecture explores how Egyptians used spoken spells, written words, images, amulets, ritual actions, and sacred substances to heal the sick, protect children, defeat enemies, communicate with the dead, and transform their spirits. Seen from an Egyptian perspective, cursing, curing, and creating were not separate domains but different expressions of a world in which magic was an expected part of everyday life.

events.name: On the Origin of Weak Magnetic Fields in Recycled Millisecond Pulsars
events.description: Theoretical work robustly predicts that the outer core of a neutron star is a superconductor. We argue that the Meissner effect in the outer core strongly suppresses magnetic field burial inside  an accreting neutron star. Consequently, millisecond pulsars likely do not contain buried fields; instead, their small magnetic dipoles imply an almost complete expulsion of the initial magnetic flux from their cores. We consider the slow magnetic field dissipation inside old neutron stars and  argue that the field can be expelled if the protons are superconducting in most of the core. The remnant field could be trapped in a small central non-superconducting part of the core, which would then determine the strength and  geometry of the millisecond pulsar field.

events.name: Asymmetric Dark Matter induced by Baryogenesis
events.description: We live in a Universe where structures are made out of baryons but not of antibaryons. Could the dark matter be made of particles and not antiparticles? This is an old question and many asymmetric dark matter scenarios have been proposed to date. Among them, the models where a dark matter asymmetry is induced from the baryon/lepton asymmetries are particularly motivated. In this seminar, I will highlight the motivations for these types of frameworks but also their challenges. I will then present a new, minimal, and predictive scenario that we developed in [2511.10731]. In this model, a dark matter asymmetry is slowly generated from the Standard Model Higgs doublet asymmetry. The scenario features two dark matter states which can lead to signals in the next generation of dark matter experiments, and we predict a new inert Higgs doublet with 46 GeV < mass < 580 GeV which can be discovered at the LHC from searches for long-lived compressed electroweak states.

events.name: Uncovering the Nature of Active Galactic Nuclei from z=0 to z=9 with Variability
events.description: Active galactic nuclei (AGN) accretion disks fuel powerful AGN feedback and are important laboratories for studying accretion physics. Because AGN are generally too distant to resolve spatially, most of what we can learn about their accretion disks comes from studying the variability in AGN light curves. However, many mysteries remain about the source of variability in AGN light curves and what this variability can reveal about the structure, internal physics, and accretion rates of AGN disks. I will show how I use radiation magnetohydrodynamic simulations, long baseline AGN light curves, and machine learning tools to improve our understanding of AGN variability and model the structure of AGN disks. These models are crucial for understanding AGN at all redshifts, including the high redshift little red dots recently discovered by the James Webb Space Telescope, which may be super-Eddington AGN.

events.name: Engineering Quantum Matter through Geometry: Twistronics and Straintronics in 2D Materials.
events.description: Twistronics and straintronics have emerged as powerful approaches for engineering lattice structures and interactions in van der Waals materials, opening new avenues toward quantum phases, emergent phenomena, and novel device functionalities. In this talk, I will present two of our recent and surprising findings on twisted and strained graphene. First, I will discuss how large-angle twisted bilayer graphene, widely assumed to be electronically trivial, can instead develop strong interlayer coupling and unexpected electronic reconstruction at the crossover between quasicrystalline and commensurate order. Second, I will present how graphene can be transformed into a flat-band, strongly correlated electronic system through our unique strain-engineering strategy, thereby creating opportunities for emergent phenomena and new quantum matters. These results highlight how twist and strain provide complementary and powerful means of reshaping electronic matter, revealing that even seemingly simple graphene can host remarkably rich and unexpected quantum phases when its geometry is strategically designed.

events.name: Hybrid Light–Matter–Spin Excitations in a van der Waals Magnet
events.description:
Magnetic materials, light, and electronic excitations can interact in ways that give rise to entirely new physical phenomena [1]. In this colloquium, I will explore one such platform: CrSBr, a layered van der Waals magnetic semiconductor in which magnetic and optical excitations are strongly coupled.
I will show that magnetic excitations or magnons, collective waves of spins in the material, leave a direct and coherent imprint on its optical response [2]. More remarkably, magnons can mediate interactions between excitons. This provides a new way to control nonlinear optical phenomena through magnetism, with spin waves acting as a knob for controlling how light interacts with light [3].
I will then turn to the dynamics of these magnetic excitations and present microwave spectroscopy of the spin-wave spectrum of CrSBr. These measurements point toward a pathway for coherent conversion between microwave and optical signals, exploiting the same exciton–magnon interactions that govern the optical response [4]. Such microwave-to-optical transduction could ultimately provide a bridge between superconducting quantum circuits, which operate at microwave frequencies, and optical quantum networks.
Together, these results illustrate how the interplay of magnetism, light, and quantum excitations in van der Waals materials can open new possibilities for controlling light with spin.[1] P. events.name: Forming low-mass neutron stars in collapsar disks
events.description: I will discuss a mechanism for forming neutron stars through gravitational instability in accretion disks produced during the collapse of massive, rapidly rotating stars. Because the Chandrasekhar mass is reduced in these neutron-rich disks, the resulting neutron stars can have sub-solar masses. Subsequent mergers between these objects, or between them and the central black hole, could produce distinctive gravitational-wave signals. Unlike conventional compact-object mergers, these events are predicted to occur in coincidence with a supernova counterpart rather than an isolated kilonova.

events.name: Synergy between Cosmology and Collider Signals from Extended Scalar Sectors
events.description: A major open question at the intersection of particle physics and cosmology is the observed imbalance between matter and antimatter. Explaining it requires a strong First Order Electro-Weak Phase Transition (FOEWPT) in the early Universe, which can be generated within New Physics (NP) scenarios with a modified Higgs potential. The rise of Gravitational Wave (GW) cosmology has made these transitions experimentally accessible, as they can induce sizeable perturbations in the primordial plasma producing a stochastic background of GWs that could be detected by future interferometers. If such a FOEWPT occurs within a specific NP framework, it will also leave characteristic signatures on scattering processes that can be probed at the HL-LHC, establishing a powerful synergy between collider searches and GW observations.  I’ll investigate this interplay within the Two-Higgs-Doublet-Model (2HDM), where the SM is augmented with a scalar doublet. This study also lays the groundwork for the exploring the cosmological vacuum evolution of the Composite-2HDM, a scenario motivated by the hierarchy problem.

events.name: Mapping the Quantum Limits of Classical Simulatability
events.description: Quantum many-body systems are significantly more challenging to simulate than their classical counterparts. This is primarily due to the quantum sign problem, which prevents a reformulation in terms of stochastically sampling classical configurations. While many “sign problem-free” models have been discovered, which admit high-accuracy numerical simulations, many believe that certain phases of matter are intrinsically sign-problematic. In this talk, I present counterexamples to a number of no-go theorems by constructing sign problem-free models for phases of matter believed to be sign-problematic, and develop a revised perspective for how one should think about intrinsic sign problems.

events.name: Electromagnetic signatures of massive black hole binary mergers and their identification in multi-messenger observations
events.description: Massive black hole binaries (MBHBs) are a natural outcome of galaxy mergers and are expected to be among the strongest sources of low-frequency gravitational waves. At sub-parsec separations, however, these binaries are extremely difficult to resolve directly. One promising approach is to search for their signatures in the time-domain variability of AGN lightcurves. Orbital motion can imprint periodic or evolving (“chirping”) signals in quasar light curves through mechanisms such as relativistic Doppler boosting. In this talk, I present a series of studies exploring methods for detecting compact SMBHBs in large optical surveys, building towards a systematic search. Using mock data motivated by the new time-domain survey LSST, we evaluate the performance of these methods. I will demonstrate that both periodic and chirping signals, consistent with GW-driven inspiral, can be identified in large optical surveys alone, and that these detections can be confirmed with even higher confidence when combined with GW observations. Finally, I will discuss a potential multi-wavelengths signature of MBHBs due to multiple disk- and jet- components.

events.name: Quantum Printing
events.description:
I  introduce Quantum Printing- a concept for controlling quantum matter by directly imprinting the quantum numbers carried by structured light (spin angular momentum, orbital angular momentum, chirality, and entanglement) onto coherent electron and magnetic states. Structured light acts as a quantum “ink” that writes, manipulates, and erases macroscopic quantum orders in both charged fluids (superconductors and quantum Hall systems) and neutral fluids (magnets), going beyond conventional thermal or magnetic control.
I will also introduce extensions of these ideas to reversible optical writing and erasing of topological skyrmions in Heisenberg magnets with THz structured beams, enabling error-corrected magnetic memory, sub-diffraction patterning, and calligraphy of continuous textures [2].Work supported by DOE DE-SC-0025580, ERC-2018-SYG 810451 HERO, KAW 2019.0068.[1]

events.name: How Dust Evolution Shapes Protoplanetary Disks
events.description:
"    Planet formation begins with the coagulation of micrometer-sized dust grains in a protoplanetary disk. This particle growth not only provides the building material for planetesimals but also shapes the environments they form in. 
    Aerodynamic drag forces between gas and dust determine how fast the grains drift and how efficiently they can be trapped in the frequently observed rings and vortices in protoplanetary disks. The size of the particles thus affects the available dust mass and composition throughout the disk. Dust also dominates the opacities and therefore regulates the thermal structure and the onset of hydrodynamic instabilities that depend on thermal relaxation. 
In my talk, I will present two recent applications of coupled multifluid simulations and dust coagulation models that capture the interplay of microphysics and large-scale dynamics in protoplanetary disks: 
    Our simulations of planet-disk systems with dust coagulation quantify the amount of small dust grains that diffuse and drift through planet-induced gaps. These calculations constrain the composition and available mass of solids in the inner disk regions.
    We furthermore investigate the effects of dust evolution on protoplanetary disk turbulence, induced by the Vertical Shear Instability. Our simulations show that efficient dust coagulation can suppress turbulence in protoplanetary disks, due to the reduced collisional cooling in the dust-depleted upper layers.
    Understanding how dust coagulation influences the dynamics of protoplanetary disks is thus key to understanding the initial conditions for planet formation and to interpreting multi-wavelength observations."

events.name: Using Tidal Disruption Events as Probes of Massive Black Hole Formation and Growth Over Cosmic Time
events.description: The tidal disruption of a star that wanders too close to a central black hole is a unique probe of quiescent supermassive black holes lurking in the nuclei of galaxies.  We have demonstrated the ability to discover and spectroscopically classify large samples of tidal disruption events (TDEs) in the optical from the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) Northern Sky Survey, with systematic high-energy follow-up with Swift and XMM-Newton. From these efforts, we now know the spectroscopic signatures, multi-wavelength properties, and host galaxy preferences of TDEs, and can begin to use TDEs as powerful probes of massive black hole demographics in quiescent galaxies.  One of the most exciting applications of TDEs is the ability to probe intermediate mass black holes (IMBHs) that are expected to reside in dwarf galaxies, with demographics that encode the seeding mechanism of massive black holes in the early Universe.  I will outline our strategy in the next decade for searching for TDEs across the black hole mass function, and over cosmic time, by extending our sensitivity to TDEs to lower central black hole masses and higher redshifts, by exploiting the discovery power of the next generation of wide-field time domain surveys, including Rubin, Roman, ULTRASAT, and UVEX.

events.name: Emulating the Bose-Hubbard Model with Arrays of Superconducting Qubits
events.description: In this talk, we study the propagation, entanglement, and entropy of quantum information using 3x3 and 4x4 arrays of superconducting qubits that emulate the two-dimensional (2D) hard-core Bose-Hubbard model. The 2D arrays feature site-selective, simultaneous control and readout of all qubits. We highlight several recent experimental demonstrations using these arrays, including quantum random walks, Anderson and Wannier-Stark localization [1], the crossover from area-law to volume-law entanglement [2], the realization of synthetic electromagnetic fields throughout the array [3], and studies of flat-band physics in rhombic lattices [4].[1] npj Quantum Information 8, 35 (2022) | arXiv:2107.05035 (2021)[2] Nature 629, 561-566 (2024) | arXiv:2306.02571 (2023)[3] Nature Physics 20, 1881-1887 (2024) | arXiv:2405.00873 (2024)[4] Physical Review X 15, 021091 (2025) | arXiv:2410.07878 (2024)

events.description: In conjunction with the Grey Art Museum’s exhibition by Alison Knowles: A Retrospective (1960–2022), on view from Sept. 9, 2026–Jan. 20, 2027. Led by computational poet Prof. Allison Parrish and artist Prof. Blair Simmons (ITP/IMA, NYU Tisch), this workshop takes inspiration from Alison Knowles’s The House of Dust (1967), one of the earliest computer-generated poems. Coded in FORTRAN, the automated combinations of materials, locations, light sources, and inhabitants that populate the stanzas of this pioneering text generate infinitely and are printed in real time on a dot matrix printer (on view at the Grey).   Participants will discover the ongoing value of Knowles’s creative methods and execute their own infinite poems. events.description: Gina KostantopoulosUCLA The ancient Mesopotamian world was populated with a wide range of demonic and monstrous creatures, all of which intersected with daily life in a variety of mostly-malignant ways. Most often, demons, or the chaotic figure of the witch, could cause serious harm, being associated with disease and illness, or even death, particularly in infants and young children.This talk will discuss some of the major threats found in Mesopotamia—the demonic, chaotic witch; the demoness Lamashtu, who was often responsible for infant mortality; and others—examining in detail how they could be safeguarded against, or actively opposed once they were believed to be present.  This lecture will take place in person at ISAW (15 East 84th Street).

events.name: What is Recorded and What is Erased: films by Maryam Tafakory
events.description: Short films by Maryam Tafakory, followed by a discussion with the director and Prof. Lelia Pourtavaf (NYU, Middle Eastern and Islamic Studies) Maryam Tafakory will share her practice working across moving image, text, and performance. Her process unfolds through long, unfinished research and gathers into constellations of speculative nonfiction pieces. She layers archival fragments, poems, newspaper clippings, audio recordings, declassified documents, and state-produced images to trace the space between what is recorded and what is erased. Maryam Tafakory is an artist-filmmaker born and raised in Iran. Her research turns to historical gaps, unspoken rules, the various practices of censorship and to the bodies, stories, and histories that are silenced or made illegible. Her work engages not only with what is missing, but with how absence itself is produced, regulated, and sustained. Her ongoing films and performances follow these regimes of control, their internalisation, and the unseen architectures that hold them in place. In dialogue with post-revolution Iranian cinema, pre-revolution censorship, and the histories of women involved in clandestine leftist groups of the 1970s, her work continues to unfold as interconnected pieces. Selected solo screenings/exhibitions include: MoMA (New York); BOZAR (Brussels); National Gallery of Art (Washington DC); Barbican Centre (London); Academy Museum (Los Angeles); Eye Film Museum (Amsterdam); e-flux (New York); Project Arts Centre (Dublin); Filmoteca de Catalunya (Barcelona); Walker Art Center (Minneapolis), Museum of the Moving Image (New York); LUX (London); among others. Selected group events include: Tate Modern (London); Cannes’ Directors Fortnight; New York Film Festival; Locarno Film Festival; Toronto International Film Festival; Villa Medici (Rome); Brooklyn Academy of Music (New York); and Anthology Film Archives (New York), among others. Her films have received numerous awards, several Oscar-qualifying, including the Gold Hugo at the 58th Chicago International Film Festival; Best Documentary Short at the 72nd Melbourne International Film Festival; the Tiger Short Award at the 51st IFF Rotterdam, and the Cinema & Gioventù Best International Short Film award at the 77th Locarno Film Festival. They have also screened at NYFF (New York), TIFF (Toronto), and BFI London Film Festival. She was a fellow at the Institute for Ideas & Imagination in Paris in 2025, and a MacDowell Fellow in 2023. She was the 2019 Flaherty/Colgate Distinguished Global Filmmaker in Residence. This event is sponsored by: The Liberal Studies Global Media Lab; The Iranian Studies Initiative; Hagop Kevorkian Center for Near Eastern Studies; The Center for Media, Culture and History; and The Center for the Study of Gender and Sexuality. events.name: Claude McKay, Wanderings of a Rebellious Poet Virtual Talkback and Film Screening
events.description: Virtual post-screening discussion and Q&A with French director Matthieu Verdeil and distinguished scholar Dr. Robert Reid-Pharr. This program is organized by the Center for Black Visual Culture and co-sponsored by NYU Institute of French Studies and NYU Department of Social and Cultural Analysis. Claude McKay, Wanderings of a Rebellious Poet (52’ - 2025 - english subtitles) film will be shared to all registrants via email with a viewing link, 48 hours in advance of the program. After 48 hours, the film will no longer be available to view. Please register BEFORE November 27th, to ensure you receive both the viewing link and webinar link. Claude McKay, Wanderings of a Rebellious Poet is a captivating voyage through the 1920s — from Harlem to Marseille, via Jamaica, Russia and Morocco — in the footsteps of Jamaican American writer Claude McKay. A rebellious voice of the Harlem Renaissance, Claude McKay spent two decades traveling the world, immersing himself in artistic and political avant-gardes while building an enduring body of work. This remarkable documentary portrait, illustrated with rare archival footage and photographs, narrated by Gaël Faye, and set to a stirring soundtrack, brings his legacy to life. For over 20 years, film director and producer Matthieu Verdeil has pursued a distinctive path at the crossroads of history, memory, and artistic creation. He collaborates with contemporary artists such as Abraham Poincheval while dedicating much of his career to rediscovering overlooked figures and movements in cultural history, including Varian Fry and Claude McKay. Verdeil first became interested in McKay in the early 2000s, recognizing him as both a pioneer of the Harlem Renaissance and a forerunner of global Black consciousness. He began extensive archival research, working with U.S. scholars Brent Hayes Edwards and French publisher Renaud Boukh (Héliotropismes). In 2021, Verdeil directed Claude McKay: From Harlem to Marseille, the first documentary devoted to the “vagabond poet.” Combining historical rigor with poetic sensitivity, the film was screened in France, the United States, Germany, the United Kingdom and beyond. Currently, Verdeil is preparing a new television film dedicated to the Harlem Renaissance, continuing his long-standing commitment to amplifying forgotten or marginalized voices whose legacies continue to shape our present, and to exploring the transatlantic fabric of Black thought. Robert F. Reid-Pharr is a Professor of Social and Cultural Analysis at New York University. He holds a Ph.D. in American Studies and an M.A. in African American Studies from Yale University as well as a B.A. in Political Science from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. He has been the Jess and Sara Cloud Distinguished Visiting Professor of English at the College of William and Mary, the Edward Said Visiting Chair of American Studies at the American University of Beirut, the Drue Heinz Visiting Professor of English at the University of Oxford, the Carlisle and Barbara Moore Distinguished Visiting Professor of English at the University of Oregon, and the F.O. Matthiessen Visiting Professor of Gender and Sexuality at Harvard University. A prominent scholar in the field of race and sexuality studies, he is the author of four books and numerous essays. His research and writing have been supported by grants from the Mellon Foundation, the National Endowment for the Humanities, the Alexander von Humboldt Foundation, the Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Studies, and the American Academy in Berlin. His work has been honored by the Publishing Triangle, the Modern Language Association and the American Literature Association. In 2015 he was inducted into the Johns Hopkins Society of Scholars and he is the recipient of a 2016 John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation Fellowship.

events.name: Darkology: Blackface and the American Way of Entertainment with Rhae Lynn Barnes
events.description: ﻿The Center for the American Experience invites you to join Rhae Lynn Barnes, Assistant Professor of History at Princeton University, and Jonathan Square, Assistant Professor of Black Visual Culture at Parsons, for a discussion of Barnes's book Darkology: Blackface and the American Way of Entertainment. Darkology is a major study of the history of blackface minstrelsy in the United States, showing how deeply it shaped American entertainment, institutions, and racial politics from the nineteenth century through the Civil Rights era and beyond. Drawing on extensive archival research, Barnes challenges the idea that blackface was marginal or short-lived, revealing instead how widely it spread across schools, churches, universities, military spaces, and public life.

events.name: Machine Stitch: A Talk on Digital Embroidery & Materiality
events.description: For New York Textile MonthWith Anette Millington, Travis Fitch, and Ragna FrodaTuesday, September 29th from 12 pm - 2 pmKellen AuditoriumRSVP is required This artist/designer talk focuses on digital embroidery in creative work, expanding industrial applications to uncover unique human sensitivities of the machine stitch. The conversation will bring together Response Patterns, a collaborative project by Anette Millington and Travis Fitch, and artist Ragna Froda, to discuss experimentation, machine collaboration, and embroidered materiality. Response Patterns is a collaborative project that leverages Anette Millington’s expertise in pattern and print, and textile embellishment, with Travis Fitch’s in-depth knowledge of digital tools, geometry, 3D-printed embellishment, and architectural design. The ongoing study of geometric and biological patterning informs their research on machine embroidery. Considering the language of patterning- units, symmetries, and algorithmic scale- they work with the embroidery machine to create tactile symbols and surfaces. Ragna Froda is an Icelandic artist, curator, and educator with a background in fashion/ textile design. Her work focuses on the process of making, working with colors and textures, and the history and culture of symbols and patterns in textiles. Ragna will discuss her “Here we go again” series of digital embroideries. The artwork, originally sketched in ink, undergoes a transformation through embroidery, guided by her assistant Bobby, the embroidery robot. As a team, they explore life events, histories, and dreams. The talk will highlight shared interests in material experimentation to expand the lexicon of machine embroidery and add emotive and temporal qualities. Examples include the use of environmentally responsive materials, such as UV-sensitive threads, and textural substrates made from fabric collage and quilting. The conversation will also focus on interventions and design processes for working with digital embroidery software and improvisation between machine and maker. Presented by MFA Textiles

events.description: Please join us for a reading with Molly McCloy (Nonfiction, 2006) as she sits down with Luis Jaramillo, Associate Professor of Writing and Chair of Fiction, to discuss her memoir Nine Grudges: The Spiteful Origins of the Happiest Dyke on Earth.About the Book:"On the cusp of her 1993 college graduation in Olympia, Molly McCloy spends her time drunk and high, pulling dykey pranks, and thrashing in mosh pits—anything to avoid the troubled, working-class family she left behind in Arizona. But after a vivid nightmare involving her dad, Molly writes him a letter, asking him to apologize for nine instances of mental, verbal, and physical abuse. She revisits each of these nine grudges before working up enough courage to mail the letter. Then, to her surprise, her dad writes back. "Nine Grudges grabs hold of you like a best friend ready to divulge terrible, wonderful secrets. Funny, soulful, absolutely unafraid to look life in the eye, Molly McCloy’s tough and tender voice is addictive. An electric debut!"—Michelle Tea, author of Knocking Myself Up "Nine Grudges shouldn’t be funny, but it is simultaneously hilarious and chilling. events.name: India China Day 2026
events.description: India China Day is a celebration of our student fellows and the broader community—an invitation for students, faculty, and staff to come together, enjoy authentic Indian and Chinese food, make new friends, exchange ideas, and learn about the fascinating research our Starr student fellows are pursuing. This year's six student fellows include three PhD students, two MA candidates, and one BFA student from across the New School for Social Research and the Parsons School of Design. Their projects span a fascinating range of topics—from exploring the production of eri silk in Assam, India, to examining people's theater in post-martial-law Taiwan and investigating women's participation in the global hair industry. Together, their projects reflect the diverse interests, perspectives, and expertise of our student community. Come celebrate our fellows, discover their research, share a meal, and find inspiration for your own research ideas. SPEAKERSAratrika Debrath: Hungry Tides: Climate Migration and Resettlement Planning in the SundarbansThis project examines climate-induced migration in the Sundarbans region spanning India and Bangladesh. Through fieldwork with displaced communities and analysis of stakeholder perspectives, it aims to produce policy solutions that support resilience and protection for climate migrants.Emily Li: Precarious Labor and Political Identity of South Asian Platform Workers in Hong KongThis project explores how South Asian food delivery workers in Hong Kong organize and resist exploitation, especially in the context of rising precarity and weakened trade unions. It focuses on how ethnic identity shapes labor activism and the possibilities for collective struggle in modern Hong Kong.Parth Patel: Off Grid Assemblies Off Grid Assemblies aims to co-design a low-cost energy kit with the community of Turtuk— a remote village in Leh, India. As an alternative to limited diesel generation, this project aims to build a decentralized, self-sufficient, and resilient off-grid electricity source for rural communities dealing with extreme climates. Nolan Young: E-Commerce as Rural Development Strategy in China — Contours of a Public-Private PartnershipThis project examines the public-private partnership model between the Chinese government and private e-commerce platforms as a rural development strategy. The project seeks to identify tangible forms of state involvement, and to understand the impacts on local communities as well as possible implications for global development.Florian Chi Zhang: Seeking Taohuayuan in a Foreign Land: Chinese New Migrants in Southeast AsiaThis project explores Chinese migration to Chiang Mai, Thailand, and how these migrants build new communities and navigate local society. Through ethnographic research, it connects this migration trend to the history of Chinese immigration in Thailand and shifting ideas of mobility, hope, and China’s global role.

events.name: Roger Kellaway, John Goldsby & Terry Clarke Autumn Reunion Masterclass
events.description: Join us for a special masterclass by the esteemed trio of Roger Kellaway, John Goldsby, and Terry Clarke. The program will focus on jazz and provide insight into the thought processes these master musicians bring to their craft. New School students will be invited to participate in the discussions and sit in with the group.Admission to attend this masterclass is free of charge as is the livestream.While you can only register for one ticket at a time further below, you may register more than once with the same email address in order to get multiple tickets.Click here to watch the livestream The masterclass kicks off an October “Autumn Reunion” of these accomplished musicians, who recorded the Live in Tokyo album in 1986. Don’t miss this opportunity to gain insight into the jazz process from practicing artists with decades of experience. There will also be a concert of this trio on October 2nd at Arnie Lawrence Hall.Artist Biographies:About Roger Kellaway: Roger is a Grammy Award winner and Academy Award nominated Pianist/Composer and has written in the fields of jazz, classical, and pop, also composing and scoring for films and television. He has worked with everyone from Ellington to Elvis, Joni Mitchell to Barbara Streisand, and Quincy Jones to Yo-Yo Ma. Roger’s commissions range from a ballet for George Ballachine and the New York Ballet to his most prized television credit, “Remembering You,” the closing theme for the groundbreaking “All in the Family” television series. In addition to leading many jazz recordings and accomplishments, he has appeared and recorded with Sonny Rollins, Wes Montgomery, Oliver Nelson, Ben Webster, Clark Terry and Bob Brookmeyer. Kellaway's jazz recordings, from In Japan (recorded in 1986) to Live at Mezzrow (released in 2024) are two of many offerings worth a listen. Roger is serving as the Musical Director for tonight's concert and resides in Ojai, California.About John Goldsby:John is a bass player and musician of extraordinary talents including his accomplishments in jazz education. He has led numerous successful recording sessions of his own and has performed with many legends including Scott Hamilton, Jay McShann, Barney Kessel, Michael Brecker, Mel Lewis, and John Lewis. During his 30-year tenure with the Grammy-winning Westdeutscher Rundfunk Big Band (WDR Big Band) he performed and recorded with McCoy Tyner, John Scofield, Joshua Redman, Ambrose Akinmusire, Roy Hargrove, Knower, Nduduzo Makhathini, and many others. John’s current album—Big Band Bass—features Bob Mintzer and WDR Big Band. The newly re-released album Tale of the Fingers — NYC 1993, also featuring Terry Clarke on drums, is heralded as a milestone album. The Jazz Bass Book is Mr. Goldsby’s classic work documenting jazz bass players and their techniques from a historical perspective. In 2025, Goldsby received the Humanitarian Award from the International Society of Bassists for his lifetime of extraordinary generosity, exceptional service and selfless devotion to the global bass community. John resides in Germany, near Cologne.About Terry Clarke:Terry is a Canadian jazz drummer who worked in the mid 60’s with the legendary saxophonist, John Handy III and is featured on the recording, Live at The Monterey Jazz Festival. Clarke then joined the Grammy-winning group, “The Fifth Dimension”, and appears with the group in the Oscar-winning Summer of Soul documentary. He later relocated to Toronto and played with luminaries such as Frank Rossolino, Lenny Breau, jazz guitar legend Jim Hall and piano icon Oscar Peterson. Jim Hall Live is generally considered one of the best jazz guitar trio recordings of the era. During this period Clarke played for 25 years with the Grammy-and Juno-winning jazz big-band, “Rob McConnell and the Boss Brass”. Clarke later worked in New York City with The Toshiko Akiyoshi Jazz Orchestra, Helen Merrill, Toots Thielemans, Red Mitchell and Roger Kellaway. Clarke is the only living drummer to be a Member of the Order of Canada (Canada’s highest civilian honour). His recording, It’s About Time, was the winner of “The Best Traditional Jazz Recording” at the 2010 Juno Awards (Canadian Grammy). Terry resides in Toronto in Canada.Producers: Producer Samuel Turvey:Sam is a founder of the Charlie Parker Jazz Festival and its producer from 1993 to 2002 and has served in the past as a Board Member of the Manna House Jazz Workshops in East Harlem and the National Jazz Museum in Harlem. Assistant Producer David Glasser:David is a long termed New School faculty member and prominent jazz alto saxophone player with many recordings in his own name and as a collaborator with Clark Terry and any number of other jazz notables. At present, he is also a member of the Count Basie orchestra. Creative Producers Pamela Shaw and Victor Talbot:Pamela and Victor had the concept of Autumn Reunion while attending a John Goldsby concert in Cologne Germany. They are responsible for selecting the musicians, suggesting the programming, and have been intimately involved in all aspects of the production. They were instrumental in securing a funding grant for this collaboration between master musicians and a university jazz program.  The Autumn Reunion concert and other related educational activities are all being presented by the New School including its production staff and by additional administrative support from Anthony C. Wood.

events.name: The Social Security Retirement Earnings Test: Should it stay or go?
events.description: Join us for the September session of the Reimagining the Economics of Aging Seminar Series, a monthly virtual forum hosted by the Wealth Equity Lab at The New School. This series brings together scholars and practitioners to deepen conversations on aging, retirement, and late-life economic security, with a focus on works in progress and active discussion. On October 7th, we will host Dr. Jason Fichtner, Senior Policy Fellow at the Center for Social Development and Executive Director of the Retirement Income Institute, Alliance for Lifetime Income. who will discuss the Social Security Retirement Earnings Test (RET).The RET was originally included in Social Security based on the straightforward social insurance concept that to receive a retirement benefit, a person must have experienced a loss in income due to retirement and no longer working. Unfortunately, the RET rules are widely misunderstood by beneficiaries today, and it discourages work in an era when earnings are an increasingly important component of old-age economic security. The RET is enormously complicated and most older workers are unaware of it -- at least until it affects them. Even when workers have heard of it, most misperceive it as a tax and think withheld benefits do not get returned. Repealing the RET could help improve the financial security of older Americans by allowing them to continue working without having some of their Social Security benefits withheld. On the other hand, repealing the RET could lead more people to claim benefits before their full retirement age and, thus, receiving a reduced monthly Social Security benefit that could worsen their financial security in older ages. Public policy decisions require an understanding of the economic and social opportunity costs and tradeoffs. Should the RET stay or should it go?

events.name: Art, Poetry, and Existence(s)
events.description: Please join us for a book launch and artist talk by Truong Tran, poet and visual artist, moderated by Margaret Rhee.  Tran's new book, How to Exi(s)t: A Poet’s Memoir, was just published by City Lights Books. Truong will discuss his art practice, his new book, and issues around queerness and resistance through poetry and memoir.About How to Exi(s)t: A Poet’s Memoir: How to Exi(s)t: A Poet’s Memoir is an experiment in nonlinear autobiography by the author of the American Book Award-winning Book of the Other, Truong Tran. Beginning in the present–at a writing residency in the aftermath of this success–How to Exi(s)t moves back and forth in time, in bursts of brief poetic essays grouped by theme. The duality of the title thematizes a dilemma at the heart of the book: how does a poet separate himself from the academic career to which he’s devoted his professional life and what does being a teacher mean outside of it?Unpeeling the layers between present and past, Tran proceeds in reverse as he explores crucial events and figures in his life, including the reaction to the publication of Book of the Other, the dynamics of whiteness and power framing his repeated rejection for a tenure track position, the profound effect of his dyslexia on his evolution as a writer and artist, the repercussions of being outed by a newspaper after winning an undergrad poetry prize, traumatic episodes growing up in the Vietnamese diaspora in San Jose, and complicated relationships with both his family and his chosen family. Attempting to fathom these experiences and connect them to his present self, Tran examines and reexamines key details rather than dispensing with them in neat anecdotes, reflecting the volatile process of imagination and memory.Unsparing, even caustic in its instance on racism as a dominant note of American life, but marked by surprising tenderness and humor, How to Exi(s)t is a compelling portrayal of Tran’s pedagogical philosophy as well as an interrogation of a poetic language that conceals as much as it reveals."Vietnamese American poet and visual artist Tran (Book of the Other) examines racism, queer history, and his own life in this striking nonlinear account."—Publishers Weekly"Tran's prose speaks directly to the reader and offers opinions and perspectives that are superbly barbed and lushly poetic all at once. . . . A wise, reflective self-portrait shimmering with genuine emotion and bracing honesty."—Kirkus Reviews

events.name: VLC Forum 2026: Conversations with the 2025–2027 Jane Lombard Fellows
events.description: In a globe-encompassing convening, the VLC Forum 2026 presents the Jane Lombard Fellows, finalists for the Jane Lombard Prize for Art and Social Justice, alongside recipient Rosana Paulino. In conversation with their nominators or invited guests, the Nepalese art collective ArTree Nepal, New York-based artist Stephanie Dinkins, Hawaiian and Samoan digital media theorist and poet Jason Edward Lewis from Canada, and Finnish artist Jenna Sutela share their nominated projects and their engagement with the material and intangible dimensions of intelligence. 12 pm | Jenna Sutela in conversation with Elvia Wilk2025–2027 Jane Lombard Fellow Jenna Sutela joins writer and collaborator Elvia Wilk to discuss a practice that moves across contemporary art, the life sciences, and emerging technologies. Drawing on more than a decade of shared dialogue, they discuss Sutela's sustained engagement with more-than-human forms of intelligence from microbes to animals to machines.Focusing on nimiia cétiï, a work that brings together biological organisms and neural networks to imagine new forms of language and relation, they reflect on how Sutela’s 2025–2027 Jane Lombard Prize for Art and Social Justice nominated project unsettles distinctions between the natural and the artificial, the biological and the computational, while opening broader questions about algorithmic governance, ecological interdependence, and the ethics of living with increasingly intelligent technologies. By positioning artistic inquiry as a site for critical experimentation, they explore how artistic practices that attend to more-than-human intelligence can challenge extractive models of innovation and offer new ways of thinking about justice across human, technological, and planetary scales. 1 pm | Lunch2 pm | Stephanie Dinkins in conversation with Neta Bomani2025–2027 Jane Lombard Fellow Stephanie Dinkins revisits her landmark project Conversations with Bina48 in a conversation with organizer and educator Neta Bomani. Since 2014, Dinkins has been in conversation with the social robot Bina48 (Breakthrough Intelligence via Neural Architecture, 48 exaflops per second), using the exchange to explore the boundaries between artificial and human consciousness through the intersecting lenses of race and gender. Nominated for the 2025–2027 Jane Lombard Prize for Art and Social Justice, Conversations with Bina48 provides the starting point for a conversation on the broader trajectory of Dinkins’ artistic practice and how Bina48 has modeled alternative ways of engaging with AI that invite us to question the racial dynamics embedded in artificial intelligence, robotics, and machine learning. Together with Bomani, they discuss technological future histories, Afro-now-ism, and the “continuum of intelligences” that encompass technology (artificial intelligence, biotechnology, and gene editing). They place this inquiry within an expanded understanding of the intelligence of natural systems, from mycelial networks to other more-than-human forms of communication and knowledge.3 pm | Jason Edward Lewis in conversation with Mashinka Hakopian2025–2027 Jane Lombard Fellow Jason Edward Lewis is joined by scholar, artist, and 2025–2027 Vera List Center Fellow Mashinka Hakopian for a conversation on Abundant Intelligences, an Indigenous-led research program and network across Canada, the United States, and New Zealand that reimagines the futures of artificial intelligence through Indigenous knowledge systems. Abundant Intelligences was nominated for the 2025–2027 Jane Lombard Prize for Art and Social Justice.Drawing on critical AI studies, anticolonial approaches to technology, and Indigenous epistemologies, Lewis and Hakopian explore how Indigenous knowledge systems, refined through millennia of community- and land-oriented intelligence, challenge dominant conceptions of intelligence and illustrate the colonial practices that inform the computational systems underpinning AI. Together they consider how technologies might be designed to work in relation with existing lifeways, sustain reciprocal relationships between interspecies worlds, and cultivate conditions of abundance rather than extraction and scarcity. Recognizing the multiplicity of ways of being intelligent in the world, their conversation asks what becomes possible when AI is designed to prioritize the flourishing of human and non-human kin alike. 4 pm | ArTree Nepal in conversation with Prabal Gurung2025–2027 Jane Lombard Fellow ArTree Nepal members are joined by Nepali American fashion designer and Parsons School of Fashion alum Prabal Gurung for a conversation exploring how artistic practice can serve as a tool for collective struggle, cultural continuity, and liberation. ArTreeNepal, a collective of five artists and curators, each from a different Indigenous background—Lavkant Chaudhary (Tharu), Hit Man Gurung (Tamu), Mekha Limbu (Yakthung), Sheelasha Rajbhandari (Newa), and Subas Tamang (Tamang)—practices contemporary art with the belief that art has deep roots in social practice. As a designer, Gurung draws on personal history, cultural identity, and fashion as a form of storytelling. In New York, Lavkant Chaudhary, Mekh Limbu, and Subas Tamang center their conversation on Tika Chhedna Angana (“A Garden of Body Markings”), the project for which they were nominated for the 2025–2027 Jane Lombard Prize for Art and Social Justice. Inspired by Indigenous tattooing practices in Nepal, the project approaches body markings as living pedagogies that weave together body, art, ecology, and community. Together, the artists and Gurung reflect on the significance of these traditions and the collective's ongoing initiatives, opening space to conditions of embodiment, Indigenous pedagogies, and the need to move beyond frameworks that exoticize or diminish lived knowledge and Indigenous worldviews.

events.description: ABOUT OLEG BEZBORODKOOleg Bezborodko is a Ukrainian pianist and composer whose works have been performed in more than twenty-five countries across Europe, North America, and Asia. His artistic path combines performance, composition, and teaching, making him one of the most versatile representatives of contemporary Ukrainian music.After studying piano and composition in Ukraine and Switzerland, he earned a Ph.D. from the Ukrainian National Academy of Music, where he currently serves as Head of the Piano Department. Alongside his academic role, he is in demand as both a chamber musician and an interpreter of contemporary repertoire. His interpretations of Valentin Silvestrov’s music, in particular, have been praised by the composer himself.Oleg’s music has been performed by leading ensembles such as musikFabrik, the Chain Ensemble, and the Kyiv Piano Duo, as well as by acclaimed soloists including pianists Stephen Gutman, Roglit Ishay, Timothy Hoft, and Dmytro Choni; violinists Dmytro Tkachenko and Orest Smovzh; and violist Tatjana Masurenko. He has collaborated with all major Ukrainian orchestras, both as a pianist and as a composer, and his works have been performed under the direction of conductors such as Andrey Boreyko, Hobart Earle, Kirill Karabits, Volodymyr Kozhukhar, Vincent Kozlowski, Ivan Ostapovych, Viktor Ploskina, Natalia Ponomarchuk, Volodymyr Sheyko, and Volodymyr Sirenko.His music has been presented at international festivals including Kyiv Music Fest, Contrasts (Lviv), Two Days and Two Nights (Odesa), Euphonie (Warsaw), Iš ARTI (Kaunas), the Biennial Festival of New Music at Florida State University (Tallahassee), INS OFFENE (Berlin), and the Brandenburgisches Fest der Neuen Musik (Potsdam).A laureate of national and international competitions, he received the Levko Revutsky Music Prize (2008) from the Ministry of Culture of Ukraine and the Mykola Lysenko Composition Award (2017). His works have been commissioned by the Goethe-Institut, the Ernst von Siemens Musikstiftung, the Ukrainian National Academic Concert Band, Musica Mundi Frankfurt,  and the Lviv Organ Hall.Since 2023, Oleg has served as Artistic Director of the “Kyiv Music Premieres” festival, one of Ukraine’s leading platforms for new music.In recent years, his orchestral works have gained particular recognition. In 2025, his Symphony Peine Del Viento (Comb of the Wind) received second prize at the San Sebastián Symphony Concours, organized by County Hall Arts in London. That same year, on June 10, his Symphony Unbroken was performed alongside Beethoven’s Eroica at the closing concert of Kharkiv Music Fest — the first symphonic concert in Kharkiv since the start of the full-scale war.Presented by Mannes Sounds Festival in collaboration with the Mannes Composition Department / Composition Forum.

events.name: VLC Matter of Intelligence Seminar 7: Intelligence, Uncertain
events.description: If intelligence has always been a contested site—attributed, withheld, performed, disputed—misinformation and disinformation reveal the political stakes of that contest in their sharpest form. The seventh seminar in the Vera List Center for Art and Politics’ Matter of Intelligence series, presented in partnership with Haus der Kulturen der Welt (HKW) as part of its Uncertain Intelligences research program, explores uncertainty in the context of contemporary cultural, political, and technological transformations. The program approaches uncertainty as a productive point of departure for reflecting on existing structures of truth and credibility, their impact on forms of knowledge and reality, and whose uncertainty counts as honest doubt and whose counts as bad faith? HKW's Uncertain Intelligences fellows, Nora Al-Badri and manuel arturo abreu, and neuroscientist and writer Suparna Choudhury consider how artistic practice might engage these conditions by holding complexity, sustaining uncertainty without surrendering to it, and refusing false clarity without collapsing into relativism. Moderated by HWK's Sara Morais dos Santos Bruss.Matter of Intelligence Seminar SeriesThrough modes of shared study, rehearsal, and iterative dialogue with invited artists, thinkers, and the public, the VLC Seminar Series develops and presents artistic and scholarly research centered on the Vera List Center’s 2025–2027 Focus Theme, Matter of Intelligence. Comprising twelve sessions convened from September 2025 through May 2027—the Seminar Series is conceived as an open curriculum and a site for collective inquiry. Each seminar is paired with a curated reader on the Matter of Intelligence Are.na channel, grounding the dialogue and opening new paths for exploration.

events.name: A Tribute to Weather Report: 50 Years of Heavy Weather
events.description: New School Studio Orchestra gives a nod to Weather Report's place in the pantheon of 20th century composers, in this genre-breaking evening that breathes new life into this legendary album.n 1977, the legendary band Weather Report released the landmark album Heavy Weather, featuring original members Joe Zawinul and Wayne Shorter, who had played together with Miles Davis, along with Jaco Pastorius, Alex Acuña, and Manolo Badrena. Fifty years later, this extraordinary group of international musicians continues to inspire and excite new generations of artists with their groundbreaking exploration of musical forms, fearless creativity and virtuosic playing. The evening includes a performance of the entire Heavy Weather album as well as a selection of other Weather Report compositions."The New School is steadily moving the center of gravity for collegiate jazz in New York further downtown." All About JazzABOUT WEATHER REPORTFormed in 1970 by keyboardist Joe Zawinul and saxophonist Wayne Shorter, Weather Report redefined the possibilities of jazz fusion by blending jazz improvisation with rock, funk, world music, and electronic textures. The band's ever-evolving lineup included legendary bassist Jaco Pastorius, whose groundbreaking approach to the electric bass helped shape the group's signature sound.Over a 16-year career, Weather Report released 14 studio albums and became one of the most influential and commercially successful jazz fusion ensembles in history. Their 1977 album Heavy Weather remains a landmark recording, featuring the iconic composition "Birdland," one of the most celebrated jazz works of the 20th century. The band's innovative music continues to inspire musicians across genres, leaving an enduring legacy in jazz and contemporary music.ABOUT THE NEW SCHOOL STUDIO ORCHESTRA (NSSO)Conducted by Keller Coker, The New School Studio Orchestra (NSSO) is composed of students from the School of Jazz and Contemporary Music and Mannes School of Music, often with guest artists, performing music from a wide variety of genres, including jazz, soul, pop, and improvised music. The thrilling U.S. premiere of Carla Bley’s Escalator Over the Hill was the epic close to the 2024–2025 season. The New York Times described the musicians as playing with “rattling intensity," adding "The sound seemed to shudder like a pot about to blow its lid." All About Jazz stated, "Presenting a cherished '70s cult jazz-rock album in its U.S. performance debut was a high-wire act of artistic bravery, yet the New School ensemble triumphed over the odds. This was very much a student performance, even if its stellar standard forced you to frequently—and delightedly—remind yourself of that improbable fact." And in the words of UK Jazz News: “The student band impressively embodied Bley’s gonzo vision. This was a worthy and deeply enjoyable ride on Escalator Over the Hill, and a historic moment to boot.”The 2025/2026 season offered a remarkable lineup, beginning with the inimitable 1930s Radio Night. The Grammy-winning Fandango at the Wall featured The New School’s Arturo O’Farrill, his Afro Latin Jazz Octet, and The Conga Patria Son Jarocho Collective. The second annual NSSO Holiday Swing ushered in the holiday season, featuring music from Ella Fitzgerald’s beloved Christmas albums and Jazz at Lincoln Center holiday arrangements, with special guest Brianna Thomas. March brought The Blue Note Records All Stars Evening, featuring James Francies, Joel Ross, and Immanuel Wilkins. All About Jazz praised the program, writing, "The New School is steadily moving the center of gravity for collegiate jazz in New York further downtown." The season culminated in May with a joyous, sold-out, dancing and singing audience at A Motown Spectacular, featuring music by The Temptations, The Four Tops, Martha and the Vandellas, Marvin Gaye, and more.  In addition, the NSSO performs annually at The Jazz Gallery.The 2026/27 Season celebrates the 40th Anniversary of the School of Jazz & Contemporary Music and a stellar New School Studio Orchestra season with A Tribute to Weather Report: 50 Years of Heavy Weather, our annual holiday show, Holiday at the Sands '66, The School of Jazz and Contemporary Music's 40th Anniversary Celebration, and to close out the season, Music and the Metropolis: a special two-night event featuring music inspired by iconic NYC buildings, monuments, and neighborhoods over 125 years, celebrating the New York architecture, neighborhoods, and spaces that have inspired more music than any other city—from Tin Pan Alley to the Brill Building to Madison Square Garden.  A collaboration with Parsons School of Design.

events.name: A Child of Our Time
events.description: What does resistance sound like? Nearly 90 years after it was written, Sir Michael Tippett’s A Child of Our Time continues to ask urgent questions about fear, injustice, division, and hope. Written in response to the rise of fascism in Europe and the violence of Kristallnacht in 1938, Tippett’s powerful oratorio for chorus and orchestra draws on African American spirituals. For Tippett, these songs expressed a universal truth: even in the face of injustice, the human spirit endures. For this one-night performance, singers from the New York Choral Society (NYCHORAL) will join the Mannes Orchestra conducted by David Hayes, with an acclaimed cast of soloists from the Mannes faculty: Laquita Mitchell, William Burden, Margaret Lattimore and Stephen Powell. Presented one week before the 2026 midterm elections, this performance invites audiences to reflect on where we have been, where we are, and the future we want to create. More than a concert, A Child of Our Time is a reminder of the power of music to bear witness, challenge injustice, and bring people together. "We are thrilled to partner with Mannes School of Music on this extraordinary performance. Bringing together the New York Choral Society’s volunteer singers with Mannes' exceptional orchestra, acclaimed voice faculty, and rising young artists is exactly the kind of collaboration that makes New York's cultural community so extraordinary. To perform a work as profound and urgently relevant as A Child of Our Time in David Geffen Hall is an incredible privilege. At a moment when many of us are searching for connection and hope, Tippett reminds us that music has the power to bear witness, challenge injustice, and bring people together. This performance lives at the intersection of art, resistance, and our shared humanity, and I can't imagine a more meaningful way to open our season." — Ellen PutneyMoore, Executive Director, New York Choral Society   ABOUT THE NEW YORK CHORAL SOCIETYThe New York Choral Society (NYCHORAL) is The Voice of the City—more than 150 auditioned volunteer singers representing every borough, profession, generation, and socio-economic background that make New York unlike anywhere else in the world. Founded in 1960, NYCHORAL is entering its 69th season with a chorus that is younger than ever: today, more than half of its singers are under the age of 35, proving that the future of choral music is already here.By day, our singers are physicians, teachers, attorneys, baristas, nonprofit leaders, engineers, artists, students, and retirees. Together, they create extraordinary performances that reflect the city they call home. Through bold programming that pairs classical masterworks with contemporary voices and ideas, NYCHORAL explores the issues shaping our world while honoring the traditions that brought us here.At NYCHORAL, we believe choral music isn't a museum piece, it's one of the most immediate ways people can come together to explore difficult questions, celebrate our shared humanity, and experience the transformative power of singing with one voice.ABOUT MANNES ORCHESTRAKnown for their bold and adventurous programming, and led by maestro David Hayes, Mannes Orchestra has been hailed by The New York Times as an orchestra whose quality is “a revelation,” and for its “intensity of focus.” The orchestra performs a multitude of concerts each season at venues including Lincoln Center’s Alice Tully Hall, David Geffen Hall, John L. Tishman Auditorium at The New School, Carnegie Hall, and performances with Martha Graham Dance Company at New York City Center, and Mannes Opera at various venues throughout the city.

events.name: An Evening with Oliver Munday
events.description: Please join us for an evening with Oliver Munday as he sits down with Sidik Fofana to discuss his books Don’t Sleep: The Urgent Messages of Oliver Munday and the short story collection Head of Household. About Don’t Sleep: The Urgent Messages of Oliver Munday:Part personal history, part design philosophy, and part advocacy, Don't Sleep: The Urgent Messages of Oliver Munday showcases the arresting work of Oliver Munday. Employing humor and menace in equal measure, Munday wields graphic design as a tool of empowerment, activism, and resistance. Drawing from the history and utility of twentieth- century agitprop, from Russian Constructivism to the Black Panthers, Munday updates a timeless medium for the social media age with his stark and often unsettling imagery.About Head of Household:From stories about a father who shows up hungover to chaperone his daughter’s kindergarten bowling trip, to another who rediscovers his love of graffiti, and a father who pays for his legal fees and apartment through his OnlyFans earnings, Head of Household is a short story collection that reckons with divorce, financial anxiety, and sexuality to create a collage of the beleaguered father, a man on the frontlines of a masculinity in crisis—stories of men salvaging the shreds of their identities while staging puppet shows and pretending to be ponies for their children.

This is a book holding spectacular spells, songs and instructions for freedom." —Terrance Hayes“…these sonnets sing the queer Black body electric with joy, with grief, with anger, and with a contagious freedom that drives me to want to dig deeper into my own body’s stories.” —Darla Himeles

events.name: The Westerlies: Works in Progress
events.description: The Westerlies, “an arty quartet…mixing ideas from jazz, new classical, and Appalachian folk” (The New York Times), hold a singular space in modern music. From Carnegie Hall to Coachella, the GRAMMY-nominated quartet has upended presumptions of the brass tradition to create music that is “folk-like and composerly, lovely and intellectually rigorous” (NPR Music). For their annual Fall Recital at The New School, the ensemble will share works in progress, including new works by members of the ensemble. ABOUT THE WESTERLIESAcross ten critically acclaimed albums, The Westerlies have earned “a unique reputation for exploring the emotional textures of American music” (DownBeat), championing living composers and collaborators including Caroline Shaw, Nico Muhly, Conrad Tao, Bill Frisell, Wayne Horvitz, and Robin Holcomb. Comprising Riley Mulherkar and Chloe Rowlands on trumpet and Andy Clausen and Addison Maye-Saxon on trombone, the ensemble has relentlessly composed, arranged, adapted, recorded, and toured over the past fifteen years with the precision of a string quartet, the audacity of a rock band, and the charm of a family sing-along.  2025 saw the release of two major recordings: Paradise, The Westerlies’ “sublime, precise, and deeply spiritual” (DownBeat) reimagination of the Shape Note choral tradition, which earned the group a GRAMMY nomination; and Songbook, Vol. 3, a live EP and concert film celebrating friends and recent collaborators including Fleet Foxes, Adrianne Lenker, Samora Pinderhughes, Anaïs Mitchell, Aoife O’Donovan, Joanna Newsom, and more. The Westerlies' singular sound and virtuosic skill have also made them in-demand collaborators, playing in studio and live alongside artists from Common to Haley Heynderickx, and on GRAMMY-nominated releases from both Fleet Foxes and Aoife O’Donovan. 2026 will see The Westerlies embark on a major retrospective of American music pioneer Bill Frisell, featuring newly composed works and arrangements; an adaptation of Maria Schneider’s GRAMMY-winning classical song cycle Winter Morning Walks, featuring South African vocalist Vuyo Sotashe; and a new collaboration with Fleet Foxes’ Robin Pecknold, exploring the music of Judee Sill.

He is the founder and director of Forensic Architecture and Professor of Spatial and Visual Cultures at Goldsmiths, University of London, where, in 2005, he founded the Centre for Research Architecture. He is the author of numerous other books, including Hollow Land, The Least of all Possible Evils, Investigative Aesthetics, The Conflict Shoreline, and Forensic Architecture. events.name: Mannes Sounds: A Celebration of the Life of Ann Schein
events.description: An all-Chopin program celebrating the life and legacy of legendary American pianist and pedagogue Ann Schein (November 10, 1939–April 16, 2026).ANN SCHEIN Ann Schein was an internationally acclaimed pianist whose remarkable career spanned more than six decades. Praised by The Washington Post for her ability to “reach right into the heart” of the music she performed, she was celebrated for her powerful interpretations of the Romantic repertoire, particularly Chopin.Following her Carnegie Hall debut as a young artist on the Sol Hurok roster, Schein performed in more than 50 countries with leading orchestras and conductors, including the New York Philharmonic, Philadelphia Orchestra, London Symphony Orchestra, George Szell, James Levine, Seiji Ozawa, and Sir Colin Davis. She appeared frequently at London’s BBC Proms and performed at the White House during the Kennedy administration.A distinguished educator as well as performer, Schein served on the piano faculty of the Peabody Conservatory for more than two decades and was an artist-faculty member of the Aspen Music Festival and School. She joined the piano faculty of Mannes School of Music in 2017, where she inspired generations of students with her artistry and mentorship.Her acclaimed discography included recordings of works by Chopin, Schumann, Carter, Copland, Debussy, and Ravel. In recognition of her contributions to music, Schein received numerous honors, including a Lifetime Achievement Award from the National Museum of Women in the Arts in 2018 and a Distinguished Alumni Award from Peabody Conservatory in 2012.Ann Schein passed away in 2026, leaving behind a lasting legacy as a pianist, educator, and mentor whose influence continues through the many musicians she inspired.

events.name: An Evening with Albert Mobilio
events.description: Please join us for a reading with Albert Mobilio as he sits down with Jennifer Firestone to discuss his new book of poems, Beginning of the Hollow. About Beginning of the Hollow:"It’s impossible to characterize Beginning of the Hollow. In the early pages, Albert Mobilio lavishes on us the spellbinding pacing of acrobatic, recursive sentences—aka his 'narrative difficulty'—which, though they include riveting observational details, 'strange turns' of syntax, understated humor, and a pentathlon of competing dictions—feel somehow like CAT scans of the soul. Then there are softly spoken introspective poems and, toward the end, a long sequence of short gnomic declarations and fragments so strikingly various in tone, so linguistically alive and entertaining, they might be renga composed by some hard-boiled detective and a lovelorn Buddhist philosopher. Charged with vivacity, totally 'unbuttoned,' psychologically alarming, and fashioned with a dexterity few poets can match, Mobilio’s Beginning of the Hollow comes fully loaded. And here you’ll find even 'better words than the words/ that make people do things.'"—Forrest Gander

events.name: Bounce: Six Balls, Six Sports and the History of Globalization
events.description: In his new book, Bounce, William Milberg, takes the game balls used in six popular sports—golf, baseball, football, soccer, tennis, and basketball—and goes deep into their complex and fascinating history, which is also the history of globalization. Each ball tells us unique and vital things about this evolution: the golf ball, for instance, uncovers the dynamics of the first wave of globalization, with colonial powers seeking rubber in the plantations of Africa, Asia, and South America, and the importance of machine technology and innovation. The football, on the other hand, shows how labor unions provided the “countervailing power” that workers needed against growing industrial corporations, prompting steady growth in pay and economic security for the average worker. Globalization has been a series of choices, in other words—by individuals, corporations, and governments. Bounce shows us how the history of these game balls helps us to understand the consequences of those choices and where we might want globalization to go. With Thomas Liess.

events.name: Sandbox Percussion performs John Luther Adams’s Prophecies of Fire.
events.description: Experience John Luther Adams’s Prophecies of Fire, which had its world premiere by Sandbox Percussion in 2024 and makes its New York premiere at The New School.ABOUT PROPHECIES OF FIRE...and I come back to findthe stars misplaced,and the smell of a world that has burned.—Jimi HendrixMy earliest musical awakening was as a drummer. From rock bands to playing timpani in a symphony orchestra, my deepest physical connections to music have been through percussion. Over the past five decades, my life’s work has led me to compose music for orchestra, string quartet, human voices, piano, electronics, and a wide variety of other media. Now, in my 70s, I’ve returned to the place where I began.Prophecies of Fire is a perpetual acceleration canon —unbroken streams of rhythm inexorably rising in pitch and growing brighter, always seeming to get faster while never quite arriving. The musicians should surround the listeners, enveloping them in a maelstrom of tones and timbres, dynamics and velocities —like the wildfires and superstorms, the turbulent seas and waves of heat now rising all around the earth. But beyond any metaphorical associations, Prophecies of Fire is a celebration of the elemental power of sound itself to touch, to move, and perhaps even to transform human consciousness.— John Luther AdamsABOUT JOHN LUTHER ADAMSFor almost forty years, John Luther Adams made his home in the boreal forest of interior Alaska, where he discovered a unique musical world grounded in space, stillness, and elemental forces.In the 1970s and into the ’80s, JLA worked full-time as an environmental activist. But the time came when he felt compelled to dedicate himself entirely to music. He made this choice with the belief that, ultimately, music can do more than politics to change the world. Since that time, he has become one of the most widely admired and influential composers in the world, receiving the Pulitzer Prize, a Grammy Award, and many other honors. In works such as Become Ocean, Become Desert, An Atlas of Deep Time, and Canticles of the Holy Wind, JLA brings the sense of wonder that we feel outdoors into the concert hall. His outdoor works such as Inuksuit, Sila: The Breath of the World, and Crossing Open Ground invite us to remember and reclaim our connections with place, wherever we may be. Now in his 70s, JLA’s deep concern for the state of the earth and the future of humanity drives him to continue composing. As he puts it: “If we can imagine a culture and a society in which we each feel more deeply responsible for our own place in the world, then we just may be able to bring that culture and that society into being.” Since leaving Alaska, JLA and his wife Cynthia have lived in the Sonoran Desert of Mexico, the Atacama Desert of Chile, and the Chihuahuan Desert of New Mexico. They now make their home in the Red Centre of Australia.ABOUT SANDBOX PERCUSSIONDescribed as “exhilarating” by The New York Times and “utterly mesmerizing” by The Guardian, the GRAMMY®-nominated ensemble Sandbox Percussion champions living composers through its unwavering dedication to contemporary chamber music. In 2011, Jonathan Allen, Victor Caccese, Ian Rosenbaum, and Terry Sweeney were brought together by their love of chamber music and the simple joy of playing together; they have since captivated audiences with performances that are both visually and aurally stunning. In 2024, Sandbox Percussion became the first percussion ensemble to be awarded the prestigious Avery Fisher Career Grant.

events.name: Fascism, Populism, and Red Pill Politics: Or Why So Many Workers Turn from Left to Right
events.description: What actually is the relationship between yesterday’s fascism and today’s right-wing populism? In his new, strikingly book, Red Pill Politics: Demystifying Today's Far Right From Fascism to Right-Wing Populism, David Ost argues that these are but two versions of a similar kind of politics that emerges during tough economic times when the Left offers no alternative and its ties to the working class weaken. Using examples from contemporary America, Europe, and Asia and from Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany, Ost explains why the Red Pill radical right is able to win the support of non-elites who traditionally align with the Left, and shows what the broad Left has done historically, and can do today, to defeat it.

events.name: Why can't our universities be free? Higher Education, Financialization and Workers' Struggle at the New School
events.description: Higher education in the US and beyond is under attack. The potential of universities to act as sanctuaries of dissent is directly undermined both by the neoliberal "restructuring" of academic institutions and by external government pressure to control and suppress dissident thought. At the same time, the mass mobilization of students, student-workers, faculty, and staff around labor rights, academic freedom, justice, and peace across the globe has once again illuminated the importance of maintaining higher education as a progressive space for critical thinking and organizing. The workers' struggle at The New School expresses many of these tensions, prompting us to ask "why can't our universities be free" and to reflect on what is required to fight back.In this hybrid event organized by the Series of Advanced Political Economy, Professor of Economics Sanjay Reddy, Professor Emeritus of Economics Richard Wolff, and ACT-UAW Local 7902 President Micaela Suminski join us for a discussion moderated by PhD Economics student Danielle Twiss.About SAPE:Sape is a joint program organized by the Economics Departments at SOAS University of London, The New School for Social Research, and the Free Institute.We launched the Series in 2022 to promote political economy beyond university walls and created a platform where academics, activists, trade unionists, and many others could come together to discuss pressing issues and explore ways to address the multi-faceted crises of our time. As of today, these lectures have collectively gained thousands of views on YouTube, in addition to the live in-person and Zoom webinar attendees.Our series has been part of the General Federation of Trade Unions (GFTU) UK, through the UK government-funded Knowledge Transfer Partnership project. With this project, we aim to connect the academic and theoretical discussions in the lecture series with workers’ struggles in the UK and internationally. The objective is to reach a wider audience, particularly the union members, leaders, and shop stewards through the GFTU’s broad network of trade unions. Our goal is to equip workers with the tools necessary for understanding macroeconomic policies and the political economy of decision-making in contemporary capitalist society. Please register to secure your seat.

events.name: Mannes Opera presents The Saint of Bleecker Street
events.description: Menotti's forgotten 1954 Broadway masterpiece won the Pulitzer and was named "Best Musical" by the NY Drama Critic's Circle. Now it finally returns to the city that inspired it.For the first time in over 15 years, Gian Carlo Menotti's Pulitzer-winning masterpiece The Saint of Bleecker Street returns to the city that inspired it. Mannes presents a homecoming for this important lost work, written for and premiered on Broadway in 1954.The following year it won both the Pulitzer Prize in Music and the New York Drama Critics' Circle Award for Best Musical (one of the few operas to ever win). The show ran for 92 performances, but has rarely been seen since. Set in Little Italy in 1954, it's a gritty, emotional drama that tells the story of a mystical young woman who has the stigmata and sees angels. Her deeply agnostic brother wants to protect her, and the neighborhood wants her to be a saint. The Saint of Bleecker Street is a propulsive drama with soaring melodies about immigrants, faith, community, and family.The production is directed by a Mannes alum, the Argentinian opera stage director and Princeton Hodder Fellow Malena Dayen, and it features a newly commissioned chamber orchestration created especially for Mannes' students. The school is thrilled to offer NY audiences a chance to see this undervalued American classic. Composer - Gian Carlo Menotti Librettist - Gian Carlo Menotti Director - Malena Dayen (Mannes alum)Performance 1 - 3/12/2027 at 7:30pmPerformance 2 - 3/13/2027 at 7:30pm

events.description: Curated by Don Wagner, a member of the Mannes Board of Governors, this concert explores the lives and music of five remarkable yet largely overlooked composers of the Tchaikovsky/Rachmaninoff era: Anton Rubinstein, Anton Arensky, Xaver Scharwenka, Georgy Catoire, and Sergei Bortkiewicz. events.name: (Un)Silent Film: PSYCHO in Concert
events.description: Experience Alfred Hitchcock’s iconic psychological thriller Psycho live in concert.From its chilling opening moments to its legendary shower scene, Psycho remains one of the most influential films in cinematic history. ABOUT THE (UN)SILENT FILM SERIES The (Un)Silent Film series has been critical in advancing the resurgence of film screenings with live music and has been hosted by Matthew Broderick, Bill Irwin, Rob Bartlett, Ed Rothstein, and Michael Bacon. (Un)Silent Film nights have presented world premieres of works composed for The Birds and The Immigrant (by Nathan Kamal and Alexis Cuadrado, respectively), a New York premiere of a score by Hollywood composer Craig Marks for Sherlock, Jr., and Charlie Chaplin’s original scores for The Gold Rush and other Chaplin classics. In Spring 2024, (Un)Silent presented the world premiere of a new score for the iconic film Metropolis, composed by Mannes student Amir Sanjari. In Fall 2024, the acclaimed Philip Glass score for Tod Browning’s 1931 classic Dracula, originally composed for the Kronos Quartet, was performed live to film by the Orange Road Quartet. The 2025–26 season continued the series’ tradition of pairing classic cinema with live music. (Un)Silent Film presented F.W. Murnau’s 1927 classic Sunrise with a modern score by Joe Kraemer, composer of film scores for The Way of the Gun, Jack Reacher, and Mission: Impossible – Rogue Nation. The season also featured The Phantom Carriage (1921), directed by and starring Victor Sjöström, with a world-premiere score by Mannes student Amir Sanjari, performed live to film by the Orange Road Quartet.

events.name: Mannes Sounds Masterclass: Vladimir Feltsman
events.description: Vladimir Feltsman was born in Moscow in 1952. He received his training at Moscow Special Music School and at Moscow Conservatory where he studied piano under the guidance of Jacob Flier. He also studied conducting in St. Petersburg (then Leningrad) Conservatory with Ilya Musin.  In 1971 he received a Grand Prix at the Margaret Long Piano Competition in Paris, and following that, toured extensively through the former Soviet Union, Europe and Japan.  In 1979, because of his growing discontent with the rigid ideological control and restrictions on artistic freedom, he applied for an exit visa from Soviet Union. In response, he was effectively banned from performing in public until he was finally granted the permission to emigrate from USSR in 1987.  His debut recital at Carnegie Hall in 1987 immediately established him as a major pianist on the American and international scene. Since then, he performed with all major American orchestras and appeared on the most prestigious recital series and music festivals in the US and abroad.  Pianist, conductor and teacher, Mr. Feltsman is recognized as one of the most probing and constantly interesting musicians of his generation. His extensive repertoire encompasses the music from Baroque to the XXI century composers and his discography includes more than 70 recordings.  He is a founder and artistic Director of PianoSummer at New Paltz, and a faculty member at SUNY New Paltz and Mannes College The New School for Music.
